## Subjective social status

Subjective social status (SSS) refers to individuals' perception of their own position in the social hierarchy [@jackman_interpretation_1973; @evans_subjective_2004]. Because information about the overall distribution is limited, people rely on heuristics to establish their own position, drawing on a subjective sample of their close reference groups [@evans_images_1992; @cruces_biased_2013]. Rather than mirroring objective resources, SSS results from a social comparison process: people assess their standing against the reference groups available to them, typically family, friends, neighbours and co-workers [@evans_images_1992; @kelley_class_1995]. Because personal networks are strongly homophilous in education, occupation and income [@mcpherson_birds_2001], these reference groups are a socially skewed sample of the wider distribution. The result is a well-documented compression towards the middle: those at the bottom tend to overestimate their position, those at the top to underestimate it, and most people identify with the middle [@kelley_class_1995; @castillo_todos_2013]. What is observed as SSS is therefore a blend of one's objective position and the position of those against whom it is judged. The literature refers to the concept as subjective social status, subjective social position [@lindemann_contextual_2014], subjective social location [@evans_subjective_2004] or subjective evaluation of social status [@slomczynski_subjective_1986], and measures it in different ways. The most widespread instrument is the MacArthur Scale of Subjective Social Status, a ten-rung ladder on which respondents place themselves relative to others in society [@adler_relationship_2000], alongside analogous top–bottom self-placement items in comparative surveys such as the ISSP [@evans_subjective_2004; @anderson_unreliable_2025].

SSS is systematically patterned by individual and contextual socioeconomic factors. At the individual level, income, educational attainment and occupational status are consistently associated with higher self-placement [@andersson_odd_2018; @chen_subjective_2018; @iturra_subjective_2018]. More recently, attention has turned to the content of work. Across 25 European countries, @andersson_occupational_2023 show that a substantial share of the variation in SSS lies between occupations, that the occupational status gradient closely follows the educational requirements of jobs, and that non-manual work carries an additional status premium over manual work. At the interpersonal level, network composition also matters: knowing more people in high-status occupations is associated with higher SSS [@kim_social_2021], and related evidence on subjective class identification shows the same pattern [@huang_subjective_2021]. At the contextual level, economic prosperity tends to raise SSS and make societies appear more egalitarian [@evans_communism_2017; @lindemann_contextual_2014; @wiesner_knowing_2025], while income inequality depresses it, particularly among the working class, and distorts how people locate themselves in the distribution [@nolan_rising_2022; @wiesner_knowing_2025].

SSS is in turn linked to attitudes towards economic inequality, particularly distributive perceptions and preferences. People who place themselves higher tend to perceive smaller income gaps and a less unequal social structure [@castillo_perception_2022; @melli_uncovering_2025], to attribute poverty to individual rather than structural causes [@schneider_poverty_2015], to legitimise existing inequalities [@buchel_objective_2021], to perceive society as more meritocratic [@iturra-sanhueza_social_2026] and to support redistribution less [@brown-iannuzzi_subjective_2015; @duman_subjective_2020; @kirsten_impact_2022]. A recurrent finding is that SSS explains these attitudes over and above objective position precisely because it captures the social comparison mechanism; when objective and subjective status diverge, the latter tends to prevail [@melli_uncovering_2025; @iturra-sanhueza_social_2026]. Research has nonetheless focused on respondents' own SSS, leaving largely unexplored how people evaluate the status of their reference groups. The reference group and reality blend hypothesis holds that status perceptions are anchored in the social position of close ties such as friends and family members [@kelley_class_1995; @evans_subjective_2004]. In a study of SSS and perceived meritocracy in Chile, @iturrasanhueza_estatus_2022 shows that the association with one's own SSS weakens once the subjective status of the family of origin and, especially, the expected future status of one's children are taken into account. Higher expected status for one's children is associated with lower perceived meritocracy, a pattern interpreted as relative deprivation stemming from spurious mobility: dissatisfaction with status attainment arising from a perceived mismatch between efforts and rewards. Market justice preferences, the view that access to social services such as education, healthcare and pensions may legitimately depend on income [@castillo_perceptions_2025], remain particularly underexplored in this respect. Little is known about how one's own SSS relates to them, and even less about the role of the subjective status of close ties, leaving a gap still to be addressed.
